**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 13, verses 1–2:**

(p. 299) **Surah al-Ra'd (The Thunder)**

**Section on its revelation**

Scholars differ over its revelation on two views:

The first is that it is Meccan (*makkiyya*, revealed in Mecca). This was narrated by ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa from Ibn ʿAbbās, and al-Ḥasan, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ and Qatāda also held this view. Abū Ṣāliḥ narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that it is Meccan, except for two verses in it: His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be struck by a calamity for what they have done...﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Ra'd: 31], and His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger."﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43].

The second is that it is Medinan (*madaniyya*, revealed in Medina). This was narrated by ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī from Ibn ʿAbbās, and Jābir ibn Zayd also held this view. It is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that it is Medinan, except for two verses revealed in Mecca, namely His saying ﴿And if there were a Qur'an by which mountains were set in motion...﴾ to the end of it [al-Ra'd: 31]. Some said: The Medinan part of it is His saying ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning﴾ up to His saying ﴿To Him is the true call﴾ [al-Ra'd: 12–14].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra.﴾ We have already discussed a body of material on the meanings of these letters in Surah al-Baqara. Three views have been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding the meaning of this expression:

The first is that its meaning is: "I am Allah, the Knowing and the Seeing," narrated by Abū al-Ḍuḥā from him. The second is: "I am Allah, the Seeing," narrated by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr from him. The third is: "I am Allah, the King, the Most Merciful," narrated by ʿAṭāʾ from him.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿These are the verses of the Book.﴾ Regarding "these" (*tilka*) there are two views, and regarding "the Book" (*al-kitāb*) there are two views, which were previously mentioned at the beginning of Surah Yunus.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that which has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth, but most people do not believe.﴾ That is, the Qur'an and other revelation. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "That is, the people of Mecca." Al-Zajjāj said: When He mentioned that they do not believe, He identified the proof that necessitates belief in the Creator, so He said: ﴿Allah is He who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾. Abū ʿUbayda said: *ʿamad* (pillars), its consonants are vocalized with a fatha, although some vocalize it with a damma, because it is the plural of *ʿamūd* (pillar), and this is the analogical form, because every word whose spelling has four letters with a third letter that is an alif, a yāʾ or a wāw, all of its plural is with consonants vocalized with a damma, such as *rasūl* (messenger), whose plural is *rusul*, and *ḥimār* (donkey), whose plural is *ḥumur*. However, there are nouns whose plurals they used with the vowel and the fatha together, such as *ʿamūd*, *adīm* and *ihāb*, and they said *adam* and (p. 301) *ahab*. The meaning of *ʿamad* is: columns, supports, and that which holds up a building. Abū Ḥaywa recited *bi-ghayri ʿumud* with a damma on the ʿayn and the mīm.

Regarding His saying ﴿you see them﴾ there are two views:

The first is that the pronoun refers to the heavens, so the meaning is: you see them without pillars. This was said by Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās, and al-Ḥasan, Qatāda and the majority also held it. Ibn al-Anbārī said: "You see them" is a new, independent statement, and the meaning is: He raised the heavens without any support holding them up. Then He said: "You see them," meaning: you witness this great matter, which makes unnecessary for you the establishment of proofs for it.

The second is that it refers to the pillars, so the meaning is: they are with pillars that you do not see. This was narrated by ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "It has pillars upon Qāf, but you do not see the pillars." Mujāhid and ʿIkrima also adopted this view. The first view is more correct.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He subjected the sun and the moon﴾, that is, He made them subservient to what is intended from them. ﴿Each runs for a specified term﴾, that is, up to a known time, which is the ending of this world. ﴿He arranges the affair﴾, that is, He directs it with His wisdom. ﴿He details the signs﴾, that is, He makes clear the signs that indicate that He is capable of resurrection, so that you may be certain of this. Abū Razīn, Qatāda and al-Nakhaʿī recited *nudabbiru al-amr nufassilu al-āyāt* with the nūn in both places.

**Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 13, verse 4:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And in the earth are neighboring tracts﴾. On this there are two opinions:

The first: they are land that is saline (*sabakhah*) and land that is sweet (*'adhbah*). One produces vegetation while the other, beside it, does not. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak.

The second: they are neighboring towns. This was said by Qatadah and Ibn Qutaybah, and it goes back to the meaning of the first.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and crops and palm trees﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Hafs from 'Asim read: "wa-zar'un wa-nakhilun sinwanun wa-ghayru sinwanin," with *raf'* (nominative) in all of them. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read ﴿and crops and palm trees, sinwanun and ghayru sinwanin﴾ with *khafd* (genitive) in all of them. Abu 'Ali said: whoever reads with *raf'*, the meaning is: "in the earth are neighboring tracts, and gardens, and in the earth is crops." Whoever reads with *khafd* takes it as referring to the vines, so the meaning is: "gardens of vines, and of crops, and of palm trees."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿sinwanun wa-ghayru sinwanin﴾. This is a description of the palm trees. Al-Zajjaj said: *sinwan* is the plural of *sinw* and *sinw*, and its meaning is that the root is one and in it there are two, three, or four palm trees. The exegetes likewise said: *sinwan* means palm trees clustered together with one root, and *ghayru sinwan* means those that are scattered. Abu Razin, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Ibn Jubayr, and Qatadah read *sununun* with a *ḍammah* on the *ṣād*. Al-Farra' said: the dialect of the people of the Hijaz is *sinwanun* with a *kasrah* on the *ṣād*, while Tamim and Qays pronounce the *ṣād* with a *ḍammah*.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They are watered with one water﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu 'Amr read *tusqa* with a *tā'*, and *nufaḍḍilu* with a *nūn*. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *tusqa* with a *tā'* as well, but they inclined the *qāf*. al-Hasan read *wa-yufaḍḍilu* with a *yā'*. 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read *yusqa* with a *yā'*, and *nufaḍḍilu* with a *nūn*, and all of them put a *kasrah* on the *ḍād*. Al-Halabi related from 'Abd al-Warith a *ḍammah* on the *yā'* in *yufaḍḍalu*, a *fatḥah* on the *ḍād*, and *ba'ḍuha* with a *raf'* on the *ḍād*. Al-Farra' said: whoever reads *tusqa* with a *tā'* has in mind the feminine form of the crops, the gardens, and the palm trees; whoever reads with a *kasrah* has in mind the plant. All of it is watered with one water, yet its fruit (*ukul*) differs: sour and sweet. In this is a sign. The exegetes said: the one water is rainwater, and the fruit (*ukul*) is the dates. Some of them are larger than others, some are better than others, some are sour and some are sweet, and so on. In this is evidence against the view of the naturalists (*al-ṭabā'iyyūn*), for if the emergence of the fruit were due to the nature of the earth, the air, and the water, then what emerges would have to be uniform, since what necessitates the emergence is uniform. When difference occurs, it indicates a capable Governor. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason﴾, that worship is not permissible except for one who is capable of this.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 5:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you are amazed﴾, meaning: at their denial and their worship of what neither benefits nor harms, after they have seen the effect of Allah's power, Mighty and Majestic is He, in the creation of things. Their denial of the Resurrection is therefore a cause for wonder. It was also said: the meaning is, if you are amazed by what you have witnessed of the adjoining pieces of land and the power of your Lord in that, then their denial of the Resurrection is amazing, because it has become clear to them from the creation of the heavens and the earth what shows that the Resurrection is easier in terms of power.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When we are dust, shall we indeed be [raised in] a new creation?﴾ Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "آيِذا كُنّا تُرابًا آيِنّا" (ā-idhā kunnā turāban ā-innā), all with the interrogative, except that Abu 'Amr lengthens the hamzah and then produces a silent yā', while Ibn Kathir produces a silent yā' after the hamzah without lengthening. Nafi' read "آيِذا" like Abu 'Amr, and there is a difference reported from him regarding the lengthening. He read "إنّا لَفي خَلْقٍ" (innā la-fī khalq) with a kasrah, as a statement. 'Asim and Hamzah read "أإذا كُنّا" and "أإنّا" with two hamzahs in them. Ibn 'Amir read "إذا كُنّا تُرابًا" with a kasrah on the alif, without interrogation, and "آإنّا," where he produces a hamzah, then lengthens, then produces a hamzah again, in the pattern of "عاعِنّا." It is also reported from Ibn 'Amir that he read "أإذا" with two hamzahs and no alif between them.

Al-aghlal (the shackles) is the plural of ghull (a shackle), and there are two views about it. The first is that they are the shackles of the Day of Resurrection, which is the view of most scholars. The second is that they are the deeds that are themselves shackles; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 6–9:

(p-305) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They ask you to hasten the evil before the good﴾. The scholars differed concerning who this verse was revealed about, in three opinions:

The first: it was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Makkah, who asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to bring them the punishment, mocking him in doing so. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it concerns the polytheists of the Arabs. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: it concerns al-Nadr ibn al-Harith when he said: "O Allah, if this is the truth from You..." This was said by Muqatil.

Concerning "the evil" and "the good" there are two opinions:

One: it is the punishment before well-being. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil.

The second: it is evil before good. This was said by Qatadah.

As for "al-mathulat" (the exemplary punishments), the majority read it with a fatha on the mim. ʿUthman, Abu Razin, Abu Mijlaz, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, al-Hasan, and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read it with a damma on the mim.

Then, concerning its meaning, there are two opinions:

One: they are the punishments. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that there has already passed (p-306) of punishment what is similar to it and what contains a deterrent, had they taken heed. Ibn al-Anbari said: al-mathulah is the punishment that leaves a blemish on the one punished by altering some part of his form, from the saying of people: "So-and-so mutilated so-and-so," when he disfigured his form by cutting off his nose or ear, or gouging out his eyes, or the like.

The second: that al-mathulat are the examples which Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, struck for them. This was said by Mujahid and Abu ʿUbaydah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: He is one who overlooks [the sins of] the polytheists when they believe, and severe in punishment toward those who persist in polytheism. Muqatil said: He is one who overlooks their polytheism in delaying the punishment, and indeed He is severe in punishment when He punishes.

Some exegetes held that this verse is abrogated by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with [in worship]﴾ [al-Nisa’: 48]. But the verifying scholars hold that it is muhkam (not abrogated), i.e., not abrogated (naskh, abrogation, being the replacement of a ruling by a later one).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ "Lawla" here means "halla" (why not). The sign they asked for was like the staff of Musa and the she-camel of Salih. They were not content with what they had seen, so Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿You are only a warner﴾, i.e., one who warns of the punishment of Allah, and you have no power over the signs.

Concerning His saying: ﴿And for every people is a guide﴾ there are six opinions:

(p-307) One: that the intended guide is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This was narrated by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and it was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and al-Nakhaʿi. The meaning would then be: "You are only the warner, and Allah is the Guide."

The second: that the guide is the caller (summoner). This was narrated by ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: that the guide is the Prophet (ﷺ). This was said by al-Hasan, ʿAta', Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd. The meaning is: "And for every people there is a prophet who warns them."

The fourth: that the guide is also the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This was said by ʿIkrimah and Abu al-Duha. The meaning is: "You are a warner, and you are a guide."

The fifth: that the guide is the deed. This was said by Abu al-ʿAliyah.

The sixth: that the guide is the one who leads to good or to evil. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The exegetes have related, through chains that do not establish the report as authentic from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, that Ibn ʿAbbas said: "When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) placed his hand on his chest and said: 'I am the warner,' and he gestured with his hand toward the shoulder of ʿAli and said: 'You are the guide, O ʿAli; through you will be guided those after me.'" The author (Ibn al-Jawzi) said: "This is among the fabrications of the Rafidah."

(p-308) Then Allah, the Exalted, informed them of His power, refuting those who deny the resurrection, and said: ﴿Allah knows what every female bears﴾, i.e., whether a clot or a lump, whether more or less, whether male or female, whether one or two or more. ﴿And what the wombs contract﴾, i.e., what they diminish, ﴿and what they increase﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions:

One: what they contract is by delivery before nine months, and what they increase is by delivery after nine months. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas, and it was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Muqatil, Ibn Qutaybah, and al-Zajjaj.

The second: what they contract is by an incomplete miscarriage, and what they increase is by a full-term child. This was narrated by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and from al-Hasan, as the two previous opinions.

The third: what they contract is by the shedding of blood during pregnancy until the child becomes small, and what they increase is when the blood is retained so the child grows. This was said by Mujahid.

The fourth: "what the wombs contract" refers to the one whom she bore before, and "what they increase" refers to the one she bears after. This was related from Qatadah and al-Suddi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And everything with Him is by measure﴾, i.e., by a decree. Abu ʿUbaydah said: it is mif'al from al-qadar (measure). Ibn ʿAbbas said: He knew every thing and determined it with precise determination.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. We have explained this in (al-Anʿam: 6). And ﴿the Great﴾ means: the Magnificent. Its meaning returns to the greatness of His station and His deserving of the attributes of exaltedness; He is greater than every great thing, because every great thing becomes small in comparison to His greatness. It is also said: "the Great" is the One who is too great to be likened to the created beings.

As for ﴿al-Mutaʿal﴾, Ibn Kathir read "al-Mutaʿali" with a ya' both in continuation and in pause, and ʿAbd al-Warith related likewise from Abu ʿAmr, (p-309) while Ibn Shanbudh related from Qunbul its affirmation in pause but not in continuation; the rest read it without a ya' in both states. Al-Mutaʿali is the One who is transcendent above the attributes of the created beings. Al-Khattabi said: it may also mean the One who is high above His creation. It is related from al-Hasan that he said: al-Mutaʿali is exalted above what the polytheists say.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whether among you is one who conceals speech﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: "Sawa'" (equal, alike) stands in place of "mustawin" (equal), and the meaning is: "equal among you." ﴿Whoever conceals speech﴾, i.e., hides it and keeps it secret, ﴿and whoever speaks it aloud﴾, i.e., declares it openly and makes it manifest. The meaning is that secrecy and openness are equal to Him.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And one who hides by night and goes forth freely by day﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: the one who hides (mustakhfi) is the one who conceals himself and is concealed in the darkness of the night, and the one who goes freely (sarib) by day is the one who is manifest and goes about his needs openly. It is said: "sarabat al-ibil yasrubu" (the camels grazed freely), when they went on the earth openly. They have recited the verse of poetry:

"I see every people have tied their stallion's tether, while we have loosed its tether, so it goes freely."

(p-310) That is, it goes away. The meaning of the speech is that the manifest and the hidden are equal to Him. This is the view of most scholars. Al-Awfi related from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿and one who hides﴾ that he said: "The one with suspicion by night; when he goes out by day, people think he is free of sin."

The second: the one who hides by night is the manifest one, and the one who goes freely by day is the concealed one. It is said: "insaraba al-wahsh" (the wild animal slipped in), when it entered its lair. This is the view of al-Akhfash, and Qutrub also mentioned it. Ibn Jarir argued for it by their saying: "khafaytu al-shay'" (I hid the thing) when you made it manifest; and from it is ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15] with the alif opened, meaning "I make it manifest." He said: "The concealed one is only called sarib because he has entered the sarab (a hole/passage) hiding himself."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 11:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For him there are successive [angels]﴾. Regarding the pronoun in "for him" (lahu) there are four opinions:

The first: it refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). This was related by Abu al-Jawza' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it refers to a king of the kings of this world. This was related by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it refers to the human being. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: it refers to God, may He be exalted. This was mentioned by Ibn Jarir and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Regarding "successive [angels]" (al-mu'aqqibat) there are two opinions:

One of them: they are the angels. This was related by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatadah and others said the same. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that for the human being there are angels who succeed one another, one coming after the other. Most of the exegetes said: they are the guardians (al-hafaza), two by day and two by night; when one group passes, another group comes after it, and they gather at the time of the Maghrib and Fajr prayers. Some people, including Ibn Zayd, said: this verse is specific to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), when 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad ibn Qays resolved to kill him, and God protected him from them, and revealed this verse.

The second opinion: the successive [angels] are the guards of kings who take turns in guarding, and this is related from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah. Al-Dahhak said: they are the polytheist sultans who guard themselves against God, may He be exalted.

Regarding His saying: ﴿They protect him by the command of God﴾ there are seven opinions:

The first: they guard him from the command of God, and cannot [prevent it]. This is according to the one who said that it refers to the polytheists who guard themselves against the command of God.

The second: the meaning is: their protection of him is from the command of God. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr, so the sense of the sentence is: this protection is part of what God has commanded them.

The third: they protect him by the command of God. This was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid and 'Ikrimah. The linguists said: the letter ba' (bi) stands in place of min, and the particles of attribute may stand in place of one another.

The fourth: they protect him from the jinn. This was said by Mujahid and al-Nakha'i. Ka'b said: Were it not that God has entrusted to you angels who ward off from you in your food and drink and your nakedness, the jinn would snatch you away. Mujahid said: There is no servant except that an angel is appointed over him who guards him in his sleep and his waking, from the jinn, mankind and vermin; when something wishes to harm him, [the angel] says: "Behind you, behind you!" except for a thing that has already been decreed for him to suffer. Abu Mijlaz said: A man from Murad came to 'Ali, peace be upon him, and said: "Be on your guard, for some people from Murad intend to kill you." He said: "With every person there are two angels who guard him from what has not been decreed. When the decree comes, they leave him to it, and the term [of life] is a strong shield."

The fifth: there is inversion and transposition in the sentence, and the meaning is: for him there are successive [angels] from the command of God who guard him. This was said by Abu Salih and al-Farra'.

The sixth: they guard him for the command of God concerning him, until they hand him over to what has been decreed for him. This was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, who cited what 'Ikrimah related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "They guard him from the command of God, until when the decree comes they leave him." 'Ikrimah said: "They guard him for the command of God."

The seventh: they record against him his good deeds and his bad deeds. This was said by Ibn Jurayj. Al-Akhfash said: The feminine form (al-mu'aqqibat) was used because of the abundance of this from them, like the words al-nassaba (genealogist) and al-'allama (very learned); then he used the masculine in His saying "they protect him" because the meaning is masculine.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, God does not change what is in a people﴾, that is: He does not strip them of His blessings ﴿until they change what is in themselves﴾, so that they act in disobedience to Him. Muqatil said: by this he means the disbelievers of Makkah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when God intends for a people an evil﴾ — regarding this there are two opinions:

One of them: that it is punishment. The second: that it is trial.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿then there is no turning it back﴾, that is: nothing can repel it, and the successive [angels] will not benefit them.

﴿And they have besides Him no protector﴾, meaning: besides God, ﴿no patron﴾, that is: no guardian who can ward off from them the punishment and the trial.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 12:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, [causing] fear and hope﴾. In this there are four opinions:

The first: [it is] fear for the traveller and hope for the resident. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas. Qatada said: "As for the traveller, he fears its harm and hardship, while the resident hopes for its benefit."

The second: [it is] fear of thunderbolts and hope for rain. It was narrated by Ata from Ibn Abbas, and al-Hasan said likewise.

The third: [it is] fear for the land that fears the harm of rain, and hope for whoever hopes to benefit from it. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: [it is] fear of punishment and hope for reward. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Ibn al-Zubayr, when he heard the sound of thunder, would say: "Indeed, this is a severe warning to the people of the earth."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He produces the heavy clouds﴾, i.e., He creates the heavy clouds laden with water. Al-Farra' said: "Although the word 'al-sahab' (the clouds) is singular in form, it is a collective noun whose singular is 'sahaba'. Its adjective was made in the plural form, as in His saying: ﴿reclining on green cushions and beautiful Abqari carpets﴾ [al-Rahman: 76], and He did not say 'akhdar' (green) or 'hasan' (beautiful)."

**The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 13, verse 13:**

(p-٣١٤) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the thunder glorifies Him with His praise﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

One: it is the name of an angel who drives the clouds, and its sound is its glorification (tasbih). This was said by Muqatil.

The second: it is the audible sound. The thunder was singled out for glorification because it is among the greatest of sounds. Ibn al-Anbari said: Describing the sound as glorifying is a metaphor (majaz), as when a speaker says: "Your speech has grieved me."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the angels, out of fear of Him﴾. Regarding the pronoun (ha' al-kinaya) there are two opinions:

One: it refers to Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, and this is the more apparent. Ibn 'Abbas said: They fear Allah, but not like the fear of the son of Adam. None of them knows who is on his right or who is on his left, and nothing distracts him from the worship of Allah.

The second: it refers to the thunder. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts (sawa'iq) and strikes with them whom He wills﴾. The commentators differed about who it was revealed concerning, and there are three opinions:

One: it was revealed concerning Arbad ibn Qays and 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl, who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ intending to assassinate him. He said: "O Allah, suffice me against them in whatever way You will." As for Arbad, Allah sent upon him a thunderbolt on a clear, sweltering day, and it burned him. As for 'Amir, a plague (ghudda) struck him and he perished. Then Allah revealed this verse. This is the view of the majority, among them Ibn Jurayj, and Arbad was the maternal brother of Labid ibn Rabi'a.

(p-٣١٥) The second: it was revealed concerning a man who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "Tell me, O Muhammad, about your God: is He a ruby? Is He gold?" Then a thunderbolt descended upon the questioner and burned him, and this verse was revealed. This was said by 'Ali, peace be upon him. Mujahid said: He was a Jew. Anas ibn Malik said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent to one of the tyrants (fara'ina) of the Arabs, inviting him to Allah, may He be exalted. He said to the messenger: 'And what is Allah? Is He of gold, or of silver, or of copper?' The messenger returned to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him. He said: 'Go back to him and invite him.' So he went back and repeated the words to him, until he returned to him a third time. While they were exchanging words, Allah sent a cloud above his head, and it thundered, and a thunderbolt fell from it, and it took off the top of his skull. Then this verse was revealed."

The third: it was revealed concerning a man who denied the Qur'an and rejected the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Allah sent upon him a thunderbolt and it destroyed him, and this verse was revealed. This was said by Qatada.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿While they dispute about Allah﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

One: they deny the greatness of Allah. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: they argue about Allah, as when one of them said: "Is He of gold, or of silver?" as has already been explained.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He is Mighty in strength (shadid al-mihal)﴾. Regarding this there are five opinions:

(p-٣١٦) One: Severe in seizing. This was said by 'Ali, peace be upon him.

The second: Severe in plotting (makr) and severe in enmity. Al-Dahhak narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: Severe in punishment. Abu Salih said it from Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid, in one narration from him, said: Severe in retribution. Abu 'Ubayda said: Severe in punishment, plotting and chastisement (nakal), and he recited for al-A'sha:

"A shoot of the nabi tree, swaying on a branch of glory, abundant in generosity, severe in mihal (strategy/might)."

"If He punishes, it is a ruin; and if He gives, He gives abundantly, and He does not care."

Ibn Qutayba said: Severe in plotting and strength, and the root of mihal is cunning (hila).

The fourth: Severe in power. This was said by Mujahid. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said: "I contended with him (mahaltuhu) with mihal," when you contend with someone until you show him which of you is the stronger, and mahal in the language means severity.

The fifth: Severe in malice (hiqd). This was said by al-Hasan al-Basri, as we have heard it from him through chains of transmission (musnad) from several routes. Several of the exegetes narrated it from him, among them Ibn al-Anbari and al-Naqqash. But this cannot be applied to the attributes of Allah, may He be exalted. Al-Naqqash said: This is a rejected view among the people of reports and of linguistic reasoning; it is not permissible that this should be one of the attributes of Allah, may He be glorified and exalted. What I choose in this matter is what 'Ali, peace be upon him, said: Severe in seizing, meaning that when He seizes the disbeliever and the wrongdoer, He does not let him escape from His punishments.

(p-317) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿To Him is the call of truth﴾ — concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: it is the word of tawhid (monotheism), which is: "There is no god but Allah." This was said by ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, and the majority. The meaning, then, is: from His creation, He has the true call. The "call" is attributed to "truth" because the two expressions differ.

The second: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is the Truth, so whoever calls upon Him calls upon the Truth. This was said by al-Ḥasan.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who call upon other than Him﴾ — i.e., the idols, which they call gods. Abū ʿUbayda said: the meaning is, "And those who call upon other than Him, apart from Him."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They do not respond to them﴾ — i.e., they do not answer them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿except like one who stretches out his palms toward the water﴾ — concerning this there are five opinions:

The first: it is the thirsty one who stretches his hand toward the well so that the water will rise up to him, but it does not reach him. This was said by ʿAlī, peace be upon him, and ʿAṭāʾ.

The second: it is the thirsty man who has placed his palms in the water, yet he does not lift them. Al-ʿAwfī narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbās.

The third: it is the thirsty one who sees his reflection in the water from afar, so he wants to reach it but cannot. Ibn Abī Ṭalḥa narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbās.

The fourth: it is the man who calls the water with his tongue and gestures to it with his hand, but it never comes to him. This was said by Mujāhid.

The fifth: it is one who stretches out his palms to grasp the water so as to bring it to his mouth, but this does not succeed for him. The Arabs say: "Whoever seeks what he does not find is like the one grasping water," and they recited:

"And I, and you, and longing for you, are like one grasping water whose fingers do not hold it."

That is, they do not carry it; al-wasq means the load. Another said:

"So I became, of what was between me and her, of affection, like the one grasping water in the hand."

This is the statement of Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn Qutayba.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error﴾ — concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: the supplication of the disbelievers to their Lord is only in error, because their voices are veiled from Allah. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbās.

The second: the worship of the disbelievers of idols is only in loss and falsehood. This was said by Muqātil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 15:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens﴾, that is, of the angels, ﴿and on the earth, of the believers﴾ ﴿willingly and unwillingly﴾.

Regarding the meaning of the prostration of those who prostrate unwillingly, there are three opinions:

The first: that it is the prostration of one who entered Islam by the sword. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: that it is the prostration of the shadow of the disbeliever. This was said by Muqatil.

(p-319) The third: that the prostration of the unwilling is his humbling himself and submitting to what Allah wills for him, of health and sickness, wealth and poverty.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and their shadows﴾, that is, the shadows of those who prostrate prostrate willingly and unwillingly. Their prostration is their inclining from side to side, and their submission to being subjected by lengthening and shortening. Ibn al-Anbari said: The lexicographers said: the ẓill (shadow) is what exists in the mornings before the sun spreads out, and the fay' (shade that returns) is what exists after the sun has declined. It was called fay' because it "returned" (fa'a), that is, it went back to the state it was in before the sun spread out. Whatever is other than that is ẓill, such as the shadow of a person, the shadow of a wall, the shadow of a garment, and the shadow of a tree. Humayd ibn Thawr said:

Neither the shadow from the cold of the forenoon can you endure, nor the shade from the cold of the evening do you taste.

And Labid said:

While the shadow was shady and pleasant, the sun rose upon it and it vanished.

And another said:

O tamarisk trees of the valley's floor, in the belly of Tuwdih, my longing for your shadows is long.

It was also said: the disbeliever prostrates to other than Allah, while his shadow prostrates to Allah. We have explained the meaning of al-ghuduww and al-asal in (al-A'raf: 7).

(p-320) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?" Say, "Allah."﴾ The question and the answer came from one side, because the polytheists did not deny that Allah is the Creator of everything. Since they did not deny it, it was as though they had answered. Then He imposed the proof upon them by His saying: ﴿Say, "Have you then taken, apart from Him, protectors (awliya')?"﴾ meaning: the idols, which you have taken as allies, worshipping them, though they possess for themselves no benefit or harm. How then could they possess it for others? Then He set forth a parable of the one who worships idols and the one who worships Allah, by His saying: ﴿Say, "Are the blind and the seeing alike?"﴾ meaning the polytheist and the believer, ﴿or are the darknesses and the light alike?﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read "tastawi" with a ta' (feminine). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read "yastawi" with a ya' (masculine). Abu 'Ali said: the feminine form is good, because the verb is feminine, and the masculine is permissible, because the feminine here is not a true feminine. By "the darknesses and the light" he means shirk and faith. ﴿Or have they set up for Allah partners who created like His creation, so that the creation seemed similar to them?﴾ Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is, "Have they set up for Allah partners who created the way He created, so that the creation of Allah became similar to the creation of these?" This is a rhetorical question of denial, and the meaning is: the matter is not so; rather, if they reflected, they would know that Allah alone is the One who creates, and no other creates anything.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Allah is the Creator of everything."﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: Say that and make it clear with the evidence you have been informed of in this surah, which indicates that He is the Creator of everything. We have already mentioned in (Yusuf: 39) the meaning of "the One, the Subduer (al-Wahid al-Qahhar)."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 17–18:

(p-321) His words, exalted is He: ﴿He sends down water from the sky﴾, meaning: the rain. ﴿So the valleys flow﴾, and awdiyah (valleys) is the plural of wadi, which is every opening between two mountains where rainwater gathers and then flows. ﴿According to their measure﴾, i.e., according to the amount they can hold. If the wadi is small, little water flows; if it is wide, much water flows. Al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Abu al-Aliyah, Ayyub, Ibn Ya'mar, and Abu Hatim, from Ya'qub, read "bi-qadarihā" (according to their measure) with the dal sukun (bi-qadrihā). His words, ﴿So the valleys flow﴾, are a figurative extension of speech; the meaning is: their waters flowed, so the modifier is omitted. Likewise His words, ﴿according to their measure﴾, i.e., according to the measure of their waters. ﴿So the torrent carries a swelling foam﴾, i.e., foam rising high above the water. This is a parable God struck. Then He struck another parable, saying: ﴿And from that which they heat in the fire﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "tūqidūna" with the ta' (you). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read it with the ya' (they). Abu 'Ali said: whoever reads with the ta', it is because of the address preceding it, which is His words ﴿Have you then taken﴾, and it may be a general address to all. Whoever reads with the ya', it is because the third-person reference has already occurred in His words ﴿Or have they set up for Allah partners﴾.

(p-322) By His words ﴿And from that which they heat in the fire﴾ He means what is put into the fire and melted of the metals, ﴿seeking an ornament﴾, meaning gold and silver, ﴿or utensils﴾, meaning iron, brass, copper, and lead, from which vessels and useful items are made. ﴿There is a foam like it﴾, i.e., when it is melted it has a foam like the foam of the torrent. This is another parable.

Regarding what these two parables were struck for, there are three opinions:

First: it is the Qur'an. Its descent from the sky is likened to water, and the hearts of the servants are likened to valleys that hold from it according to the measure of certainty and doubt, intellect and ignorance, so it settles within them. The believer benefits from what is in his heart as the earth benefits in which the rain settles, while the disbeliever does not benefit from the Qur'an because of his doubt and disbelief. So what he acquires of the Qur'an is like the foam and the dross of iron, from which no benefit is gained.

Second: it is truth and falsehood. Truth is likened to the water that remains pure, and falsehood is likened to the foam that departs. Although it rises above the water, it will be annihilated; likewise falsehood, even if it prevails over truth in some circumstances, God will surely nullify it.

Third: it is a parable God struck for the believer and the disbeliever. The believer's belief and deed are like the water that is beneficial, and the disbeliever's belief and deed are like the foam.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Thus﴾, i.e., just as this was mentioned, God strikes the parable of truth and falsehood. Abu 'Ubayda said: thus God depicts the truth and depicts the falsehood.

As for jufa' (scum), Ibn Qutaybah said: it is what the valley casts to its sides. It is said: the pot cast off its foam when it threw it from itself. Ibn Faris said: jufa' is what the torrent has cast away, and from it the word jafa' (estrangement) is derived. Ibn al-Anbari said: ﴿jufa'an﴾ means decayed and scattered. Ibn 'Abbas said: when the foam is touched, it is nothing.

(p-323) His words, exalted is He: ﴿And as for what benefits people﴾, of the water and the substances whose foam has departed, ﴿it remains in the earth﴾ and is benefited from, ﴿thus﴾ the truth remains for its people.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿For those who responded to their Lord﴾, meaning the believers, ﴿and those who did not respond to Him﴾, meaning the disbelievers. Abu 'Ubayda said: istajabtu laka and istajabtuka are the same, and it has the meaning of ajabtu (I answered).

Regarding al-husna (the best reward), there are three opinions:

First: it is Paradise. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and the majority. Second: it is life and provision; this was said by Mujahid. Third: it is every good from Paradise and what is below it; this was said by Abu 'Ubayda.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Even if they ransomed themselves with it﴾, i.e., they would have made it a ransom for their souls from the punishment, and it would not be accepted from them. Regarding su' al-hisab (evil reckoning), there are three opinions:

First: it is scrutiny of their deeds; this was narrated by Abu al-Jawza' from Ibn 'Abbas. al-Nakha'i said: it is that one is reckoned for all of his sins, so none of them is forgiven.

Second: that no good deed from them is accepted, and no evil deed of theirs is overlooked.

Third: it is rebuke and reproach at the reckoning.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿والَّذِينَ صَبَرُوا﴾ أيْ: عَلى ما أُمِرُوا بِهِ ﴿ابْتِغاءَ وجْهِ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ أيْ: طَلَبًا لِرِضاهُ ﴿وَأقامُوا الصَّلاةَ﴾ أتَمُّوها ﴿وَأنْفَقُوا مِمّا رَزَقْناهُمْ﴾ مِنَ الأمْوالِ في طاعَةِ اللَّهِ. قالَ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ: يُرِيدُ بِالصَّلاةِ: الصَّلَواتِ الخَمْسَ، وبِالإنْفاقِ: الزَّكاةَ.

Translation of the Qur'anic verse: "And those who are patient, seeking the countenance of their Lord, and establish the prayer (ṣalāh, the ritual prayer), and spend out of what We have provided for them."

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَيَدْرَءُونَ﴾ أيْ: يَدْفَعُونَ ﴿بِالحَسَنَةِ السَّيِّئَةَ﴾ . وفي المُرادِ بِهِما خَمْسَةُ أقْوالٍ:

Translation of the Qur'anic verse: "And they repel evil with good." That is, they push away evil with good. Regarding what is meant by these two, there are five opinions:

أحَدُها: يَدْفَعُونَ بِالعَمَلِ الصّالِحِ الشَّرَّ مِنَ العَمَلِ، قالَهُ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ. والثّانِي: يَدْفَعُونَ بِالمَعْرُوفِ المُنْكَرَ، قالَهُ سَعِيدُ بْنُ جُبَيْرٍ. والثّالِثُ: بِالعَفْوِ الظُّلْمَ، قالَهُ (p-٣٢٥)جُوَيْبِرٌ. والرّابِعُ: بِالحِلْمِ السَّفَهَ، كَأنَّهم إذا سُفِهَ عَلَيْهِمْ حَلُمُوا، قالَهُ ابْنُ قُتَيْبَةَ.

The first: they repel evil deeds with righteous deeds, said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: they repel wrongdoing with what is right, said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr. The third: they repel injustice with forgiveness, said by Juwaybir. The fourth: they repel foolishness with forbearance, as if when they are treated foolishly they show forbearance, said by Ibn Qutaybah.

وَالخامِسُ: بِالتَّوْبَةِ الذَّنْبَ، قالَهُ ابْنُ كَيْسانَ.

The fifth: they repel sin with repentance, said by Ibn Kaysan.

**"And they rejoiced in the worldly life"** — Ibn ʿAbbas said: he means the polytheists of Makkah; they rejoiced in what they gained of the world, so they transgressed and denied the Messengers.

**"And the worldly life, in comparison with the Hereafter, is nothing but a fleeting enjoyment"** — that is, in comparison to it (bi-l-qiyas ilayha), **"nothing but a fleeting enjoyment"** (mata') — that is, like a thing that one enjoys, and then it perishes.

**Ibn al-Jawzi, Zad al-Masir, on Surah 13, verse 27:**

Allah's words: ﴿And those who disbelieve say﴾ were revealed concerning the polytheists (mushrikūn) of Makkah when they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for signs like those given to the prophets. ﴿Say: Indeed, Allah leads astray whom He wills﴾ means: He turns him away from guidance, just as He turned you away after the signs had been sent down to you and deprived you of reflecting upon them. ﴿And guides to Himself whoever turns back in repentance﴾ means: whoever returns to the truth. Only one whom Allah wills to return to the truth returns to it, so it is as if He had said: "And He guides whom He wills."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 28–29:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who believe﴾. This is a substitute (badal) for His saying: ﴿who turns (anaba)﴾, and the meaning is: He guides those who believe, ﴿and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah﴾. Regarding this remembrance there are two opinions:

One of them: it is the Qur'an. The second: the remembrance of Allah in general.

Regarding the meaning of this tranquillity (tuma'nina) there are two opinions:

One of them: it is love for Him and intimacy with Him. The second: calm reliance upon Him without doubt, in contrast to those who, when Allah is mentioned, have their hearts recoil (ishma'azzat).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Surely in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "Ala (alā) is a particle of alerting and inception, and the meaning is: the hearts that are the hearts of the believers find rest, because the disbeliever's heart is not at rest."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Blessed (tuba) is for them﴾. Concerning it there are eight opinions:

The first: it is the name of a tree in Paradise. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is Tuba?" He said: "A tree in Paradise, a journey of a hundred years; the garments of the people of Paradise come forth from its sheaths." Abu Hurayra said: Tuba is a tree in Paradise, to which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: "Split open for My servant whatever he wishes," so it splits open for him to produce horses with their saddles and bridles, camels with their reins, and whatever garments he wishes. Shahr ibn Hawshab said: Tuba is a tree in Paradise, all the trees of Paradise have branches from it, from beyond the wall of Paradise. This is the view of 'Atiyya, Shammar ibn 'Atiyya, Mughith ibn Sumayy and Abu Salih.

The second: it is the name of Paradise in Abyssinian (Habashi), narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. The author (Ibn al-Jawzi) said: I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur, from Sa'id ibn Masjuh, who said: Tuba is the name of Paradise in Hindi. Among those who held that it is the name of Paradise is 'Ikrima, and from Mujahid there are two similar reports.

The third: the meaning of "tuba lahum" is joy and coolness of the eye for them, narrated by 'Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: its meaning is bounty (ni'ma) for them, said by 'Ikrima in one narration, and in another narration from him: "What a blessing for them."

The fifth: felicity (ghibta) for them, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak.

The sixth: its meaning is good for them, said by al-Nakha'i in one narration, and in another from him he said: the good and the honour which Allah has given them. Ma'mar narrated from Qatada, who said: a man says to another, "Tuba laka," meaning: you have attained good; and it is an Arabic expression.

The seventh: a good end (husna) for them, narrated by Sa'id from Qatada from al-Hasan.

The eighth: the meaning is a pleasant life for them. According to the grammarians, "Tuba" is fu'la from al-tayyib (good), this is the saying of al-Zajjaj. Ibn al-Anbari said: its interpretation is the pleasant state and the delightful condition, and its original form is "tuybā," and the ya' became waw because it is quiescent and the letter before it is dammah, just as it became in "muqin" whose original is "muyqin," because it is derived from yaqin (certainty), so the damma overcame the ya' in it and made it a waw.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and a good place of return (husn ma'ab)﴾. Ma'ab: the place of return and the place of turning back.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 30:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Thus have We sent you﴾, that is: just as We sent the prophets before you.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions:

The first: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the disbelievers of Quraysh, 'Prostrate to the Most Merciful (al-Rahman),' they said, 'And what is al-Rahman?' So this verse was revealed." It was said to them: the Most Merciful whom you deny is my Lord. This is the statement of al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: When they were drafting the treaty of al-Hudaybiyah, 'Ali (peace be upon him) wrote, "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." Suhayl ibn 'Amr said, "We do not know al-Rahman except Musaylimah." So this verse was revealed. This was related by Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj, and Muqatil.

The third: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was one day in al-Hijr supplicating, and Abu Jahl was listening to him while he was saying, 'O Rahman!' So he turned back, retreating to the polytheists, and said, 'Muhammad used to forbid us from worshipping the gods, and yet he calls upon two gods!' So this verse was revealed." This was mentioned by 'Ali ibn Ahmad al-Nisaburi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and to Him is my return﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is a verbal noun (masdar) of "tubtu ilayhi" (I turned in repentance to Him).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 31–32:

(p-330) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if only a Qur'an by which mountains were set in motion, or the earth were split open by it, or the dead were made to speak...﴾ The occasion of its revelation: the polytheists of Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If you would widen for us the valleys of Makkah with the Qur'an, and set its mountains in motion so that we may cultivate them, and bring back to life those of us who have died..." So this verse was revealed. Al-Awfi related it from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam said: Quraysh said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Call upon Allah to move these mountains away from us, and to make the earth flow with rivers for us so that we may plant, or to bring our dead back to life so that we may speak with them, or to turn this rock into gold so that it may make us independent of the journey of winter and summer. Indeed the prophets had signs." So this verse was revealed, and there was revealed also His saying: ﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them﴾ [al-Isra' 17:59]. The meaning of His saying ﴿or the earth were split open by it﴾ is: it was cleft and made into rivers. ﴿Or the dead were made to speak by it﴾ means: they were brought back to life until they spoke.

They differed concerning the answer (jawab) of "law" (lau, "if") on two views.

The first: it is omitted. Regarding the estimated meaning of the speech there are two statements. One: its estimate is "this Qur'an would have been [the cause]"; this was mentioned by al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah. Qatadah said: "If this were done with a Qur'an other than your Qur'an, it would be done with your Qur'an." The second: its estimate is "If all this were the case, they would still not have believed."

(p-331) Its evidence is His saying: ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels...﴾ to the end of the verse [al-An'am 6:111]. This was stated by al-Zajjaj.

The second: the answer of "law" is placed first, and the meaning is: "while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful. And if We had sent down to them what they asked..." This was also mentioned by al-Farra'.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Rather, to Allah belongs the affair entirely﴾ means: if He willed that they believe, they would believe; and if He does not will it, what they proposed of signs will not benefit them. Then He emphasized this by His saying: ﴿Have not those who believed despaired?﴾ and concerning it there are four statements:

One: "Have they not then become clear (afalam yatabayyan)?" Al-Awfi related it from Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Ikrimah related from him that he used to read it thus and would say: "I think the scribe wrote it while he was drowsy." This is also the view of Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Abu Malik, and Muqatil.

The second: "Have they not known (afalam ya'lam)?" Ibn Abi Talhah related it from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd said likewise. Ibn Qutaybah said: "It is said that it is a dialect of the Nakha' tribe, where *yay'as* means *ya'lam* (knows)." The poet said:

Say to them in the mountain pass when they capture me: "Did you not know (alam tay'asu) that I am the son of Faris Zahdam?"

The word "despair" was used in place of "knowledge" because, in knowing a thing and being certain of it, one despairs of anything else.

(p-332) The third: the meaning is: "Those who believed have indeed despaired that they would guide anyone; and if Allah willed, He would have guided all people." This was stated by Abu al-'Aliyah.

The fourth: "Have not those who believed despaired that these polytheists would believe?" This was stated by al-Kisa'i. Al-Zajjaj said: "The meaning, in my view, is: Have not those who believed despaired of the faith of these people whom Allah described as not believing, because if He had willed, He would have guided all people?"

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be struck by a calamity﴾ — concerning them there are two statements:

One: they are all the disbelievers; this was stated by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The second: the disbelievers of Makkah; this was stated by Muqatil.

As for *al-qari'ah* (the calamity), al-Zajjaj said: it is linguistically the severe disaster that descends upon a great matter.

Concerning what is meant by it here there are two statements:

One: it is a punishment from the sky; al-Awfi related it from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: the expeditions and advance parties that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would dispatch; this was stated by 'Ikrimah.

Concerning His saying: ﴿Or it settles close to their dwellings﴾ there are two statements:

One: it is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); the meaning is: "Or you, O Muhammad, settle close to them." Sa'id ibn Jubayr related it from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, and Qatadah said likewise.

The second: it is the calamity (al-qari'ah); this was stated by al-Hasan.

Concerning His saying: ﴿Until the promise of Allah comes﴾ there are two statements:

One: it is the conquest of Makkah; this was stated by Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil. The second: it is the Resurrection; this was stated by al-Hasan.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 33:

Allah's saying: ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned﴾ means: Himself, Mighty and Majestic. The meaning of "standing over" (al-qiyam) here is: taking charge of the affairs of His creation, managing their provision and their terms (of life), counting their deeds for recompense. The meaning is: Is He who recompenses every soul for what it has earned, rewarding it when it does good and seizing it for what it committed, like those idols that do not have this attribute? Al-Farra' said: its response (jawab) has been omitted, because the meaning is known, and He has made it clear after this in His saying: ﴿And they have set up partners with Allah﴾, as if it were said: "like their partners."

Allah's saying: ﴿Say: Name them﴾, i.e., by what they deserve of attributes and of the ascription of acts to them, if they are partners of Allah, just as Allah is named "the Creator," "the Provider," "the Giver of Life," and "the Bringer of Death." And if they named them with any of these, they would be lying.

Allah's saying: ﴿Or will you inform Him of what He does not know in the earth?﴾ This is an interrogative (istifham) disconnected (munqati') from what precedes it. The meaning: if they name them with the attributes of Allah, then say to them: "Will you inform Him", i.e., will you tell Him of a partner for Him in the earth, while He does not know of a partner for Himself? Had there been one, He would have known it.

Allah's saying: ﴿Or by an outward saying?﴾ Concerning it there are three opinions:

One: "Or by a conjecture of speech," said by Mujahid. Second: "by falsehood," said by Qatadah. Third: "by words that have no basis and no reality."

Allah's saying: ﴿Rather, the scheming of those who disbelieved has been made attractive to them﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: Satan made disbelief attractive to them.

Allah's saying: ﴿And they were barred from the way﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir recited "wa-saddu" (وصَدُّوا) with a fatha on the ṣād, and the like of it in (Ḥā Mīm, the Believer) [Ghafir: 37]. 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited "wa-ṣuddū" (وصُدُّوا) with a ḍamma in both places. Whoever reads with fatha means: they barred the Muslims, either from faith or from the Sacred House. Whoever reads with ḍamma means: Allah barred them from the way of guidance.

The words of the Most High: ﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world﴾, which is killing, captivity, and sickness. So for them there is punishment in this world, and for the believers it is an expiation (kaffarah, a means of atonement for sins). "And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe," meaning more intense. ﴿And they will have no protector from Allah against it﴾, meaning no one to shield them from His punishment.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 35:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The parable of Paradise﴾, i.e., its description: that rivers flow beneath it. This is the view of the majority (al-jumhur). Tha'lab said: the predicate (khabar) of "parable" is implied before it, and the meaning is: "In what We describe to you is the parable of Paradise, and in what We relate to you is the report (khabar) of Paradise." ﴿Its food is everlasting﴾. Al-Hasan said: he means that its fruits do not cease, unlike the fruits of this world, "and its shade" because it does not pass away, and the sun does not abrogate (tansakhuhu) it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That is the final outcome (ʿuqba) of those who have taqwa﴾, i.e., the end of their affair is their arrival at it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 36:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those to whom We have given the Book﴾ — concerning this there are three opinions:

(p-335) The first: they are the Muslim Jews. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas. Muqatil said: they are 'Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions.

The second: they are the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This was said by Qatadah.

The third: they are the believers among the People of the Book, both Jews and Christians. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. As for ﴿that which has been sent down to you﴾, it is the Qur'an, in which the Muslims rejoice and confirm it, and the believers among the People of the Book rejoice in it, because it confirms what is with them. It has also been said that 'Abdullah ibn Salam and those among the People of the Book who believed with him were distressed by the scarcity of mention of al-Rahman in the Qur'an while it was frequently mentioned in the Torah. When His mention was revealed, they rejoiced, while the polytheists denied Him, and so this verse was revealed.

As for ﴿the factions﴾ (al-ahzab), they are the disbelievers who banded together against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in hostility. Concerning them there are four opinions:

The first: they are the Jews and the Christians. This was said by Qatadah. The second: they are the Jews, the Christians and the Magians. This was said by Ibn Zayd. The third: the sons of Umayyah, the sons of al-Mughirah, and the family of Abu Talhah ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza. This was said by Muqatil. The fourth: the disbelievers of Quraysh. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Concerning that part of it which they denied, there are three opinions:

The first: it is the mention of al-Rahman, the Resurrection, and Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Muqatil.

The second: they recognised the sending of the Messenger in their scriptures, but denied his prophethood.

The third: they recognised his truthfulness but denied affirming it. Al-Mawardi mentioned these last two.

And thus We have sent it down: that is, just as We sent down the Books to the prophets in their own languages, We have sent down the Qur'an to you as "a judgment in Arabic" (ḥukman ʿarabiyyan). Ibn ʿAbbas said: he means the obligations (farāʾiḍ) contained in it. Abu ʿUbayda said: "a religion in Arabic" (dīnan ʿarabiyyan).

[p. 336] His saying, Exalted is He: "And if you were to follow their desires," there are two opinions concerning it:

The first: in your prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis, "after the knowledge has come to you" that your qibla is the Kaaba. This was said by Ibn al-Sāʾib.

The second: in accepting what they call you to of the creed (millah) of your fathers. This was said by Muqatil.

His saying, Exalted is He: "You will have no protector from Allah, nor any" (mina llāhi min walīyin) — that is: you will have no one near from the punishment of Allah who benefits you, "nor any defender" (wa-lā wāqin) who protects you.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 38:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have certainly sent messengers before you and appointed for them wives and descendants.﴾ The occasion of its revelation: the Jews reproached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for having many wives. They said, "If he were a prophet as he claims, prophethood would have occupied him from marrying women." So this verse was revealed. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The meaning of the verse is that the messengers before you were humans who had wives, meaning women, and offspring, meaning children. ﴿And it was not for a messenger to bring a sign except by permission of Allah.﴾ That is, by His command. This is a reply to those who proposed signs to him.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For every term there is a decree (kitab).﴾ Regarding it there are three opinions:

The first: for every term among the terms of creation there is a decree with Allah. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: it is from the inverted order (al-muqaddam wa'l-mu'akhkhar), and the meaning is: for every book that descends from the heavens there is a term. This was said by al-Dahhak and al-Farra'.

(p-337) The third: for every term that Allah, mighty and majestic, has decreed, and for every matter that He has decided, there is a decree in which it is recorded, and no sign or anything else occurs except by a term that Allah has decreed in a decree. This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn Jarir.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 39:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah erases what He wills and establishes﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read "wa-yuthbitu" with the thā' unvowelled (sākinah) and the bā' light (khafifah). Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "wa-yuthabbitu" with the bā' doubled (mushaddadah) and the thā' vowelled with a fatha (maftūḥah). Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) said: The meaning is "wa-yuthabbituhu" (and He establishes it). He dispensed with transitivizing the second verb because the first of the two verbs was already transitive.

The exegetes differed over what is meant by "He erases and establishes," and they gave eight opinions:

The first: it is general, covering provision, term of life, happiness and wretchedness. This is the view of 'Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Wa'il, al-Dahhak and Ibn Jurayj.

The second: it refers to abrogating and the abrogated (naskh), so He erases the abrogated and establishes the abrogating. This meaning was transmitted by 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, al-Qurazi and Ibn Zayd also held it. Ibn Qutaybah said: "Allah erases what He wills" means that He abrogates from the Qur'an what He wills, "and establishes" means that He leaves it firmly in place without abrogating it, and this is the clear (muhkam) verse.

The third: He erases whatever He wills and establishes, except for wretchedness and happiness, and life and death. Sa'id ibn Jubayr transmitted this from Ibn 'Abbas. The evidence for this view is what Muslim reported in his Sahih from the hadith of Hudhayfah ibn Usayd, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "When forty-five nights have passed over the drop of semen, the angel assigned to it says: 'Male or female?' Then Allah decrees, and the angel writes. He says: 'Wretched or happy?' Then Allah decrees, and the angel writes. He says: 'Its deeds and its term?' Then Allah decrees, and the angel writes. Then the scroll is rolled up, and nothing is added to it or subtracted from it."

The fourth: He erases whatever He wills and establishes, except that wretchedness and happiness do not change. This was said by Mujahid.

The fifth: He erases the one whose term has come and establishes the one whose term has not come. This was said by al-Hasan.

The sixth: He erases from the sins of His servants whatever He wills, so He forgives them, and establishes whatever He wills, so He does not forgive them. This was transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The seventh: He erases what He wills through repentance and establishes good deeds in its place. This was said by 'Ikrimah.

The eighth: He erases from the registers of the recording angels (al-hafaẓah) what has no reward or punishment in it, and He establishes what has reward or punishment in it. This was said by al-Dahhak and Abu Salih. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: All speech is written down, until on Thursday everything in it that has no reward or punishment is discarded, such as your saying "I ate," "I drank," "I entered," "I left," and the like, and this is true; and He establishes what carries reward and punishment.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: It is the origin of the Book. The exegetes said: It is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), in which is recorded what will happen and what will come into being. Abu al-Darda' transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah, in the three hours that remain of the night, looks into the Book, which no one other than Him looks into, and He erases whatever He wills and establishes." Ikrimah transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: They are two books: a book other than the Mother of the Book, from which He erases whatever He wills and in which He establishes, and the Mother of the Book is with Him, and nothing in it is changed.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whether We show you some of what We promise them﴾, meaning: of the punishment, while you are alive, ﴿or We take you in death﴾ before We show you that. So upon you is only to convey [the message], ﴿and upon Us is the reckoning﴾. Muqatil said: it means the recompense. Ibn Abi Talha narrated from Ibn Abbas that His saying, ﴿So upon you is only the conveying [of the message]﴾, was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword and the obligation of jihad. Qatadah also said this.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 41:

(p-340) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts?﴾ Concerning it there are five opinions:

The first: it is what Allah grants His Prophet (ﷺ) of the land. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan and al-Dahhak also said this. Muqatil said: "﴿Do they not see﴾ means the disbelievers of Makkah. ﴿that We come to the land﴾ means the land of Makkah. ﴿reducing it from its outlying parts﴾ means what surrounds it."

The second: it is the town being ruined until only the houses remain on its side. This was narrated by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Ikrimah also said this.

The third: it is the reduction of its people and its blessing. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. al-Sha'bi said: it is the reduction of lives and fruits.

The fourth: it is the passing away of its jurists and the best of its people. This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fifth: it is the death of its people. This was said by Mujahid, 'Ata', and Qatadah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah judges; there is none to repel His judgment.﴾ Ibn Qutaybah said: no one overturns it by changing or diminishing it. We have explained the meaning of swiftness of reckoning in Surat al-Baqarah (2:202).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 42:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And those before them had already plotted﴾ means: the disbelievers of the earlier nations plotted against their prophets, intending to kill them, just as the Quraysh plotted against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to kill him. ﴿To Allah belongs all planning﴾ means: the planning of planners is created by Him, and it harms only by His will; and in this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and reassurance for him. ﴿He knows what every soul earns﴾ of good and evil, and no harm befalls except by His permission.

"وسَيَعْلَمُ الكافِرُ" (And the disbeliever will know): Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr recited it as "al-kafir" in the singular. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means Abu Jahl. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-kafir" here is a noun of genus (ism jins). ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited it as "al-kuffar" in the plural.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿For whom is the good outcome of the abode﴾ means: for whom is Paradise at the final end of the matter.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 13, verse 43:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieve say﴾ — concerning them there are two opinions:

One: they are the Jews and the Christians. The second: they are the disbelievers of Quraysh. ﴿Say: "Sufficient is Allah as a witness"﴾, meaning, a witness ﴿between me and you﴾, by what He has made manifest of the signs and made clear of the proofs of my prophethood.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ — concerning it there are seven opinions:

One: they are the scholars of the Jews and the Christians; this was related by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: he is 'Abd Allah ibn Salam. This was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Ibn Zayd, Ibn al-Sa'ib, and Muqatil.

The third: they are a group from the People of the Book who used to bear witness to the truth, among them 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, Salman al-Farisi, and Tamim al-Dari. This was said by Qatadah.

(p-342) The fourth: he is Jibril (peace be upon him). This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The fifth: he is 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. This was said by Ibn al-Hanafiyyah.

The sixth: he is Binyamin. This was said by Shammar.

The seventh: he is Allah the Exalted. This was related from al-Hasan and Mujahid, and al-Zajjaj chose it and argued for it by the reading of one who recited: "Wa-min 'indihi 'ulima al-kitabu" (with 'ulima in the passive and al-kitabu in the nominative). This is the reading of Ibn al-Sumayfa', Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Mujahid, and Abu Haywah. And the narration of Ibn Abi Suraij from al-Kisa'i: "Wa-min" with a kasra on the mim, "'indihi" with a kasra on the dal, "'ulima" with a damma on the mim, a kasra on the lam, and a fatha on the mim, and "al-kitabu" in the nominative. And al-Hasan recited "Wa-min" with a kasra on the mim, "'indihi" with a kasra on the dal, "'ilmu" with a kasra on the 'ayn and a damma on the mim, "al-kitabi" in the genitive as a construct phrase, as if he said: it was revealed from the knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
